title: The spirit of the law
hookLine: the rules serve the aims: life, mind, faith, family, property

cards: Can a starving man eat what the law forbids? Say a traveler is lost in the desert, days without food, and the only thing in reach is meat he may not eat. Does he starve with clean hands?

The Qur'an has already answered, in surah two, right after listing what is forbidden. In Pickthall's words: "But he who is driven by necessity, neither craving nor transgressing, it is no sin for him."
The rule bends because it was there to serve something, and here that something is his life.

teach.b: Muslim jurists gave this a name: the maqasid al-shari'ah, the aims of the law.

Al-Ghazali, in his book on legal theory, al-Mustasfa, says the law protects five things: religion, life, mind, lineage and property. Later, the Andalusian scholar al-Shatibi built a whole study around these aims.
Take each one and a rule comes into focus.
Faith: the law protects worship and forbids forcing it; the Qur'an says there is no compulsion in religion. Life: the ban on killing, and the starving traveler's permission.
Mind: the ban on wine and other intoxicants, which cloud judgment. Family, or lineage: marriage, the rights of children, the bride's gift.
Property: the honest merchant, the clear contract, the ban on riba, the fixed shares of inheritance.

Seen this way, the rules of the last two weeks look less like a list and more like a house, every room built to protect something. Scholars use the aims two ways. When texts are clear, the aims explain them.

When a new case arrives with no text, like the hospital corridor, the aims guide the reasoning. They also warn against the opposite mistake: using the aims to throw out clear rules whenever they feel inconvenient.
The aims serve the texts; they don't replace them. But asking what a rule is for, the jurists say, isn't disrespect. It's how they read.

how: Muslim scholars use the maqasid al-shari'ah, the aims of the law, to explain existing rules and to guide reasoning on new questions, while holding that the aims serve the texts rather than replace them.

the private intention behind each person's prayer

games.q: you're lost in the desert, days without food. the only thing in reach is meat the law forbids. what does surah two say?
o: eat what you need, neither craving nor transgressing; it is no sin.
eat it, and make up for it with a fast.
games.why: the verse says one driven by necessity, neither craving nor transgressing, commits no sin: the rule serves life.

practice: Pick one rule from the last two weeks, the wet grain on top, the third by will, the camel's fair load, and ask which of the five it protects: faith, life, mind, family or property.
Then try a rule of your own, no phones at dinner, pay on time, pray at dawn, and notice whether it looks different once you can see what it's guarding.

wordCard.voice: The spirit of the law. The maqasid, the aims the rules serve: protecting faith, life, mind, family and property, as al-Ghazali names them. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: aims, purposes; in law, the purposes the shari'ah serves.

carryVoice: Your line: the aim behind it. Every rule is guarding something. Go gently.
